stories.title: UKMTO says bulk carrier struck in Hormuz
stories.summary: UKMTO says bulk carrier struck in Hormuz A bulk carrier has been struck by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz,  the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said. UKMTO said it received a verified report that the projectile hit the vessel’s hull. "The crew is reported safe, no damage assessment has been reported, and environmental impact is unknown at present," the UKMTO wrote on X, advising vessels to transit the area with caution and report any suspicious activity. sentences.text: A bulk carrier has been struck by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said.

"The crew is reported safe, no damage assessment has been reported, and environmental impact is unknown at present," the UKMTO wrote on X, advising vessels to transit the area with caution and report any suspicious activity.
UKMTO said it received a verified report that the projectile hit the vessel’s hull.

stories.title: Solar eclipse inspires talk of Pac-man and Shinto myths
stories.summary: People across the South West gathered to watch a rare solar eclipse on Wednesday evening. The event began at approx 19:00 BST with the Moon passing between the Earth and the Sun, creating a crescent shape in the sky. In Sidmouth, families gathered to watch the event, with children describing it as a "once in a lifetime opportunity" and others comparing the shape of the Sun to a banana. One young girl, Charlotte, said: "It's really exciting because the next time I'll see one, I'll be a lot older. It's like a once in a lifetime opportunity." Charlie described the atmosphere as "magical", and said: "The kids haven't stopped screaming and been dancing around since we've been here." Some people marked birthdays and anniversaries during the eclipse, giving the evening a romantic significance. One young girl named Alice described the eclipse as brilliant, and said: "It kind of looks like Pac-man", whilst another felt that the sun disappearing was "kind of scary". Commander Dave Lee, Royal Navy Parachute Display Team, spent the event parachuting into Pendennis Castle at the beginning of the eclipse. Lee was one of five members of the Royal Navy and Royal Marines jumping out of the small aircraft at about 6,000ft (1829m), before deploying their colourful canopies. Lee said: "It is really a once in a lifetime experience, you have a very real feeling of immediacy and freedom, and you get a great view." David Heathfield spent the event telling stories about the "rare" mythology surrounding eclipses, in particular, the story of Amano-Iwato - the Japanese goddess of the sun - who hid in a cave depriving the world of light.
